facts.text: The whispering gallery has tiled arches; people in opposite corners can hear each other speaking quietly.
The information booth in the Main Concourse has a four-faced clock.
It is a railway terminal at 89 East 42nd Street in Manhattan.
Oak leaf and acorn decorations reference the Vanderbilt family, who financed the terminal.

explanation: The whispering gallery, the information booth’s four-faced clock, and East 42nd Street all point to Grand Central Terminal.

facts.text: The park has a marble arch honoring George Washington.
Its fountain is a popular meeting place and is older than the arch.
The park has a tradition of chess playing.
It is in Manhattan, at Fifth Avenue, Waverly Place, West 4th Street and Macdougal Street.

explanation: The Washington Arch, the fountain, chess players, and the streets around the park identify Washington Square Park.

facts.text: This public park runs along a 1.45-mile elevated freight rail structure on Manhattan's West Side.
The original railway lifted freight trains about thirty feet above crowded city streets.
The final train traveled the route in 1980 carrying three carloads of frozen turkeys.
Sections of the original train tracks are incorporated into the park's planting beds.

explanation: An elevated West Side rail structure, tracks among plantings, and a final frozen-turkey shipment identify the High Line.

facts.text: Its observation experience spans the 67th, 69th, and 70th floors of an Art Deco skyscraper.
The upper terraces offer unobstructed 360-degree views of the New York City skyline.
A famous seasonal skating rink sits below the complex's equally famous Christmas tree.
The central tower rises seventy floors and roughly 850 feet above Midtown Manhattan.

explanation: The three-level observation deck, Art Deco tower, skating rink, and Christmas tree identify Rockefeller Center.

facts.text: Completed in 1883, this crossing first linked Manhattan to the city across the East River.
Its stone neo-Gothic towers are recognizable by their tall pointed arches.
Emily Warren Roebling helped oversee the work and ensured the project reached completion.
Pedestrians travel above the East River with Lower Manhattan visible behind the cables.

explanation: The 1883 East River crossing, neo-Gothic arches, cables, and Emily Warren Roebling identify the Brooklyn Bridge.

facts.text: A massive Croton water reservoir once occupied the eastern side of this Midtown public space.
The New York Public Library's main building replaced that reservoir in 1911.
The glass-and-iron Crystal Palace exhibition hall opened beside the site in 1853.
Long before its lawn and movable chairs, part of the site served as a potter's field.

explanation: The former Croton Reservoir, the adjacent New York Public Library, the Crystal Palace, and the lawn identify Bryant Park.
